name: Grimlock
rows: Grimlocks are a pathetic race, descendent from humans craven enough to worship the illithid race as deities. That said, their wretchedness can still prove useful to the rest of us. Generations of exposure to the illithid's experiments and influence has produced a permanent physiological change in the brain of the grimlock that when brewed into a potion, can provide some level of immunity to the abilities of the mind flayers.

name: Grung
rows: Unfortunately, the poison of a grung is neutralized shortly after being harvested and is thus effectively useless. The poison gland however still possesses trace enzymes and chemicals that create a mild hallucinogenic when brewed long enough. Some yuan-ti tribes that live near grung tribes have been found with clay pots full of this hallucinogenic drink, ostensibly for ceremonial purposes.

name: Grung Elite Warrior
rows: Unfortunately, the poison of a grung is neutralized shortly after being harvested and is thus effectively useless. The poison gland however still possesses trace enzymes and chemicals that create a mild hallucinogenic when brewed long enough. Some yuan-ti tribes that live near grung tribes have been found with clay pots full of this hallucinogenic drink, ostensibly for ceremonial purposes.

In jungles occupied by grung, the echo of their distinctive chirr can be heard no matter where one goes. The chirr is most dangerous when elicited by their elite warriors, denoted by their orange or gold hues. These grung possess a series of membranes kept in a sack below their chins that when warbled appropriately, creates a more mesmerizing tune that can dull the senses of the unaware. Some craftier bards have taken to using these sacks in musical instruments that can create some of the same mesmerizing and hypnotic tones.

name: Grung Trinket Table
rows: {@dice 1d4} days' worth of {@item rations (1 day)|PHB|rations} (swamp roots and critters)
{@dice 1d4} binds made from swamp plant fibers

name: Grung Wildling
rows: Unfortunately, the poison of a grung is neutralized shortly after being harvested and is thus effectively useless. The poison gland however still possesses trace enzymes and chemicals that create a mild hallucinogenic when brewed long enough. Some yuan-ti tribes that live near grung tribes have been found with clay pots full of this hallucinogenic drink, ostensibly for ceremonial purposes.

name: Grymclover Forests; Becoming Lost
intro: Finding your way through a forest that's been mutated like this is exceptionally difficult due to the dense brambles, thick canopy, and low visibility. When a character makes a Wisdom ({@skill Survival}) check to navigate to a specific location within the forest, consult the {@table Grymclover Forests; Grymclover Navigation DCs|GriffonsSaddlebag2|Grymclover Navigation DCs} table. On a failed check, they become lost and suffer a setback determined by the {@table Grymclover Forests; Becoming Lost|GriffonsSaddlebag2|Becoming Lost} table.
rows: Completely lost, the party gets turned around and ends the day at the edge of the forest where they initially entered.
Confused and wandering, the party ends the day up to {@dice 2d4} miles in a random direction away from their intended destination for that day.
Despite getting lost, the party recovers and ends the day only {@dice 1d4} miles away from their intended destination for that day.

name: Grymclover Forests; Corrupted Creatures
intro: Beasts, monstrosities, and even plants that venture into a grymclover forest will sometimes become suffused by the area's corrupting magic, twisting them with mystifying effects. At your discretion, you can use the following table to determine how a creature may have been warped by the corruption.
rows: The creature can use a bonus action to turn {@condition invisible}, as if by the {@spell invisibility} spell.
The creature can use an action to cast a 1st-level spell at will, such as {@spell bane}, {@spell entangle}, {@spell inflict wounds}, or {@spell magic missile}.
The creature regains 5 hit points at the start of its turn if it has at least 1 hit point. If the creature takes radiant damage, this trait doesn't function at the start of its next turn.

The creature is covered in dense brambles, which grant it a +2 bonus to AC and deals {@damage 1d6} piercing damage to any creature that {@action grapple|PHB|grapples} it or is {@condition grappled} by it at the start of each of its turns.

The creature has telepathy out to 120 feet and is aware of the presence of creatures within that range that have an Intelligence score of 4 or higher. It knows the distance and direction to each creature.

The creature has increased pain tolerance, gaining 30 temporary hit points whenever it finishes a short or long rest. If another creature hits it with a melee attack while it has these hit points, the attacker takes 5 necrotic damage.

name: Grymclover Forests; Corrupted Foraged Food and Drink
intro: The adverse effects that cause a grymclover forest to emerge provide additional danger by corrupting sources of clean water and food. A foraging character makes a DC 15 Wisdom ({@skill Survival}) check. There's a {@chance 50|50 percent} chance that any food or water found in these forests has been corrupted. A DC 15 Intelligence ({@skill Nature}) or Wisdom ({@skill Survival}) check or {@spell detect poison and disease} spell reveals if any foraged food or water has been corrupted. A creature that ingests corrupted food or water in this way must roll on the Corrupted Foraged Food and Drink table.
rows: The creature is {@condition poisoned} for {@dice 3d4} hours, even if they would normally be immune to the {@condition poisoned} condition.
The creature is {@condition poisoned} for 1 hour, even if they would normally be immune to the {@condition poisoned} condition.
The creature gains no beneficial effects from the food or water but suffers no other ill effects.

name: Grymclover Forests; Corruptive Influence
intro: The manipulative energy that corrupts a forest into a grymclover one can linger for centuries, if not longer. Such twisted magic can wrack the minds of travelers with doubts and fears. Characters within a forest must succeed on a DC 13 Intelligence saving throw whenever they finish a long rest or suffer from an effect from the Corruptive Influence table below. A character has disadvantage on saving throws against these effects if it is within 3 miles of a gateway to the plane of the Fey or the realm of shadows and dread. A corruptive influence lasts until the creature finishes a long rest or is targeted by the {@spell greater restoration|PHB} spell or similar magic.
rows: Your senses betray you, making it difficult to accurately judge or feel confident of your surroundings. For the duration, you have disadvantage on Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) checks and Intelligence ({@skill Investigation}) checks.

Your feelings of aggression and mistrust are heightened. For the duration, you gain the following flaw, "I can only trust myself. If someone crosses me, I will defend myself by whatever means necessary."
You are overcome with sorrow and grief, threatening your hope and sense of self. For the duration, you have disadvantage on Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws.

You have the overwhelming feeling of being watched from the shadows at all times, preventing you from recovering from a short rest. For the duration, whenever you expend a Hit Die to regain hit points, roll the die twice and use the lower result.

name: Grymclover Forests; Example Dungeons Table
rows: A spiraling, spiked tower built by a legendary necromancer, such as Dendallen ({@link saddleb.ag/dendallen}), or an ancient {@creature lich}.
Roving bands of mindless undead loosely controlled by {@creature wight|MM|wights}, an inexperienced necromancer, or other powerful undead.
The grove and accompanying settlement of an old {@creature druid} circle that worshipped a wrathful, primeval god of nature.
Acolyte {@creature druid|MM|druids} follow the footsteps of their spiritual or literal ancestors, working to summon an avatar of their deity to the Material Plane.
A complex of huts and cottages belonging to a coven of {@creature green hag|MM|green hags} that dabbled in magic forbidden even by others of their kind.
One or more young {@creature green hag|MM|green hags} or {@creature dryad|MM|dryads} tapping into the corruptive enchantment for power and knowledge.
The lair of a powerful {@creature ancient green dragon} trained in druidic magic.
A mixture of {@creature kobold|MM|kobolds}, {@creature cultist|MM|cultists}, and {@creature cult fanatic|MM|cult fanatics} attempting to resurrect a long-dead dragon by any means necessary.
The ruined capital city of a nation of ambitious elves that delved too deeply into the arcane and druidic magic of ecological transmutation.
Various hostile plant life and even some sentient plant creatures nourished and empowered by the residual corruption of the forest.
A sprawling and decrepit estate manor, where a cruel {@creature vampire} reigned by blood and terror.
A group of {@creature vampire|MM|vampires} and their surviving spawn have fled from crusaders, plotting and preparing their vengeance.
A camp from which a terrifyingly large and vicious {@creature gnoll} band terrorized a vast swathe of the surrounding region.
{@creature Bandit|MM|Bandits} or other scavengers are using the dungeon as their base of operations, but the forest's magic is causing them to mutate.
Ruins containing a still partly active summoning circle, where an infamous diabolist released dozens of devils and demons into the world.
A jagged tear in reality itself is allowing various fiends to cross from the Lower Planes onto the Material Plane, potentially heralding a massive invasion on the horizon.

name: Grymclover Forests; Example Grymclover Jungle Random Encounter Table
rows: An arch of slowly-shifting brambles that acts as a gateway to the plane of the Fey ({@chance 50|50%}) or the plane of Shadow ({@chance 50|50%}) during a waxing crescent moon or new moon, respectively.
A {@creature grymhare|GriffonsSaddlebag2} (see Grymclover Stat Blocks) innocently lying in a stray sunbeam to lure in unwary prey.
A circle of {@dice 4d4} {@creature druid|MM|druids} that are developing a ritual to channel ({@chance 75|75%}) or cleanse ({@chance 25|25%}) the Grymclover Forest's corruption.

{@dice 1d10} {@creature gray ooze|MM|gray oozes} ({@chance 45|45%}), {@dice 1d6} {@creature ochre jelly|MM|ochre jellies} ({@chance 35|35%}), or {@dice 1d3} {@creature black pudding|MM|black puddings} ({@chance 20|20%}) milling about aimlessly.

{@dice 1d4} corrupted, predatory beasts ({@chance 60|60%}) native to the region, such as {@creature brown bear|MM|bears} or {@creature wolf|MM|wolves}, or corrupted dinosaurs ({@chance 40|40%}) like {@creature triceratops} or {@creature tyrannosaurus rex} (see {@table Grymclover Forests; Corrupted Creatures|GriffonsSaddlebag2|Corrupted Creatures} sidebar above).

The brambles of the forest encircle the party to impede travel. Each character must succeed on a DC 14 Constitution saving throw or take {@damage 2d6} piercing damage and gain one level of {@condition exhaustion} from the constricting vegetation.

{@dice 1d10} {@creature bramble creeper|GriffonsSaddlebag2|bramble creepers} (see Grymclover Stat Blocks) ({@chance 50|50%}) or {@dice 2d8} {@creature archer flower|GriffonsSaddlebag2|archer flowers} (see Grymclover Stat Blocks) ({@chance 50|50%}) patiently waiting in ambush.

{@dice 3d4} {@creature awakened shrub|MM|awakened shrubs} ({@chance 40|40%}), {@dice 1d10} {@creature awakened tree|MM|awakened trees} ({@chance 30|30%}), or {@dice 1d4} {@creature shambling mound|MM|shambling mounds} ({@chance 30|30%}) originally made from the forest's natural plant life, but now corrupted by the forest's choking brambles.

{@dice 2d12} {@creature psybird|GriffonsSaddlebag2|psybirds} (see Grymclover Stat Blocks) ({@chance 50|50%}) or {@dice 1d4} {@creature cloverback toad|GriffonsSaddlebag2|cloverback toads} (see Grymclover Stat Blocks) ({@chance 50|50%}) stirring up mist and fog with their movements.

A {@creature grym-mage tyrannosaur|GriffonsSaddlebag2} (see Grymclover Stat Blocks) ({@chance 50|50%}) or {@dice 1d8} {@creature cyglops|GriffonsSaddlebag2} (see Grymclover Stat Blocks) ({@chance 50|50%}) hunting and scavenging, respectively.

The swirling mists thicken and grow acidic for the next {@dice 1d4} hours. At the end of each hour, a character must succeed on a DC 16 Constitution saving throw or take {@damage 4d8} acid damage unless they are protected by shelters such as a tent, building, or another fog-proof barrier.

An unexpected dungeon or ruin (see {@table Grymclover Forests; Example Dungeons Table|GriffonsSaddlebag2|Example Dungeons Table}) that is younger than the forest's corruption ({@chance 80|80%}) or is the origin of it ({@chance 20|20%}).

name: Grymclover Forests; Grymclover Navigation DCs
intro: Finding your way through a forest that's been mutated like this is exceptionally difficult due to the dense brambles, thick canopy, and low visibility. When a character makes a Wisdom ({@skill Survival}) check to navigate to a specific location within the forest, consult the {@table Grymclover Forests; Grymclover Navigation DCs|GriffonsSaddlebag2|Grymclover Navigation DCs} table. On a failed check, they become lost and suffer a setback determined by the {@table Grymclover Forests; Becoming Lost|GriffonsSaddlebag2|Becoming Lost} table.
rows: A location on the outskirts of the wood, or near a larger settlement
A location near the center of the forest or steeped in Corruption, like most dungeons and ruins are
A location that is lost or hidden, such as a portal to the Fey or Shadow planes, a secret settlement, or a magically cloaked dungeon or ruin

name: Guard Drake
rows: The blood of a guard drake greatly resembles that of a real dragon, however its luster is noticeably dulled, and it is much more viscous than the famously free-flowing dragon blood. While it contains much less magical potential, guard drake blood apparently smells enough like regular dragon blood to confuse a dragon's sense of smell, thus giving rise to its use in certain dragon baits/repellents.

As a guard drake is formed of a dragon's scales, it is no wonder that their own scales resemble that of their progenitors'. They are however, of a much lower quality, and are more reminiscent of the smooth scales of a snake than the heavy plates of a real dragon's. While they are useless for making more guard drakes or for making armor, they can be used for stylish sets of clothing in the striking hues of the chromatic dragonflights.

entries: A guard drake's heart is one of the only truly magical organs in its body as it shares an innate connection with the dragon that created it. With a bit of magical altering, it can be used to track dragons wherever it goes.

entries.name: Use:
entries: If you cast the {@spell locate creature} spell on this heart once per day for 10 consecutive days, it becomes permanently enchanted and reacts to the presence of dragons that are the same color as the guard drake from whom this heart was taken. While enchanted in this way, the heart will begin to beat while it is within 1,000 feet of that color of dragon, with the heart beating steadily faster the closer that dragon is.

name: Guardian Domain Spells
rows: {@spell protection from evil and good|PHB}, {@spell sanctuary|PHB}
{@spell guardian of faith|PHB}, {@spell Otiluke's Resilient Sphere|PHB|resilient sphere}

name: Guardian Naga
rows: Virtually identical to the bones of an ordinary serpent, except on a larger scale. When ground up into a powder and then brewed into a tea however, it creates an intoxicating drink that some cultures have used for spiritual purposes. Those that have drunk it have claimed visions of long-forgotten histories, but they are inevitably forgotten once the drink has left their system.

Nagas are renowned for their rejuvenation abilities, and this property transfers to their scales. Indeed, powdered naga scales are one of many potential catalysts required when brewing the ubiquitous healing potion.

Nagas require no glands to produce their venom as their fangs remain venomous even when the naga is reduced to a skeletal form. Proper extraction and then re-smithing allows these fangs to serve as powerful weapons with an extra poisonous punch. Beware though, as a revived naga may not take kindly to the idea of a mortal running around with one of their teeth.

entries: (0 if willingly given by the guardian naga)

The heart of a guardian naga may be taken by force, but it is only useful when given freely by the benevolent creatures. When eaten, the recipient gains the naga's rejuvenation ability for at least one death. In exchange, the naga's own cycle of rebirth is temporarily halted. A guardian naga only does this when it sees great potential in a mortal creature and wishes to be a part of that creature fulfilling their destiny.

entries.name: Use:
entries: If the naga heart is taken and eaten under the free and willing permission of the guardian naga, the eater temporarily gains the ability to return to life after death. If the eater dies, they will return to life in {@dice 1d6} days and regain all hit points, missing body parts, and be cured of all non-magical diseases. Only a {@spell wish} spell can prevent this trait from functioning. In addition, the naga from whom the heart was taken loses its rejuvenation ability until the creature that ate their heart returns to life for the first time using this ability. After the eater returns to life for the first time using this ability, they lose this ability.

name: Guild Work
rows: Modest lifestyle for the week + 5 gp per day of work
Comfortable lifestyle for the week + 10 gp per day of work
Wealthy lifestyle for the week + 20 gp per day of work
Aristocratic lifestyle for the week + 50 gp per day of work.

name: Guild Work Complications
rows: A customer cancels an order, reducing your earnings for the week by one category.
You work for a lucrative contract, increasing your earnings for the week b one rank category.
Your tools are damaged or stolen, forcing you to buy new ones.*
An incident occurs in the workhall for which you are blamed (justified or not, as you choose). You are barred from the workhall for the next 6 workweeks.*
You are accused of selling runestones outide of guild channels by a colleague.*
A runestone bearing your magical signature was used to commit a crime.*
footnotes: * Might involve a rival.

name: Guildhalls: Amenities
intro: Many guilds offer additional services to members through common areas, and can provide unique spaces for social scenes during an adventure. These should be customized with elements relevant to the guild type.
rows: Meeting Space: Every guild, even those who do not yet own their own building has a meeting space. It is essential to the planning and organizing of the guild. This is generally a hall with chairs or benches, but can take the form of anything from a raked theatre to a small tavern space. Members generally enter this space ready to hear news and take part in the guilds plans. Speaking within the guild meeting space makes it easier to gain information and favors.

Common Area/Libations: An area for relaxing, distinctly separate from where the meetings are held. This may also serve as a dining area or hall to host events. Examples are a tavern area, lounge or library. A guild member who spends an hour at rest in this area may better resist the next adversarial effect.

Training Area: Most members of a guild have their own space to practice their craft but even masters come together sometimes to improve. This space has everything needed to work on the trade and generally has a few members poking about to offer commentary. A guild member working here can easier pratice his craft. Members generally need to provide their own raw materials or pay for any materials used.

Barracks: Lodging is anything from a space by the fire to individual guest rooms. Prosperous guilds may even be willing to put up the travelling companions of their members. This is very useful when the guild has chapters in several cities. A guild with a barracks provides free lodging to its members.

Protection/Storage: The number one problem with a warehouse is keeping thieves out of it. A guildhall with this amenity has an area to store the possessions and goods of its members. It may also take extra measures to protect its grounds, such as high walls, complicated locks or patrolling guards.

Contracts/Information: This may be a message board, an archive or a lounge where the older members gather to share wisdom. Members making use of this amenity can make it easier to complete tasks relevant to the guild's purview.

name: Guildhalls: Initiations
intro: Guilds do far more than serve as a meeting place for idle talk. Their schemes can be grand and sometimes treacherous. Even joining a guild can be a dangerous endeavour. Use these tables to add adventure and mystery to a guild.

{@b Benefits:} Once gained, membership comes with several benefits. The starting attitude for a fellow guild member is generally one step more favourable than normal. Guild members generally offer a 10% discount on their goods or services to other members and have contracts set up to offer the same discount on merchandise that is common to their profession. See "{@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenities}" for more benefits a guild may provide.

{@b Dues:} Guilds generally also require something in return of its members. It's generally not more than a few silver a month in membership dues and being kept apprised of information relevant to the guild's interest. Adventuring members are generally excused from making monthly visits to pay dues and in return are expected to take up the occasional task for the guild leaders.

{@b Initiations:} What a commoner or even an adventuring hero needs to do to join the guild. Many guilds have several levels of initiation, with primary membership being easy but not granting full benefits
rows: A letter of note from a community leader.
The sponsorship of an active guild member.
Tithe 10% of current wealth to the guild's patron temple.
Have recently assisted a local community member.
Complete a moderate test of skill in the guild's area of expertise.
Complete an expert test of skill in the guild's area of expertise.
Complete a moderate test of knowledge about the guild's history.
Complete a minor task for the guild, such as picking up an order from a distant member.
Apprentice under a full member, and earn their personal approval.
Travel to the capital and study under one of the guild masters.
Travel across the continent and learn from as many members as possible.
Swear a blood oath of loyalty to the guild often at the height of some esoteric ceremony.
Recruit a new customer for exclusive contract to the guild.
Recite from memory the guild charter, after a night of feasting and heavy drink.
Seek out a rare component of the guild's craft and present it to the guild leaders.
Defeat a member of a rival guild in a public contest of skill.
Kill an existing member, earning their place.

name: Guildhalls: Makeshift Guildhall
rows: A dank basement with mould growing on the walls.
The second floor apartment above the guild leader's shop.
A few tables pushed together in a local tavern, with members shouting to be heard over the rabble.
The corner table in the local tavern, after regular hours
A private backroom in the local tavern with a two drink minimum.
The centre of the city park, in full view of the public eye.
The alley between the butcher and the general goods store.
The front room of a general store, after business hours.
The backroom of a general store, crates piled high and smelling of yeast.
A warehouse, dimly lit by low lanterns.
An empty tenement, smelling of urine.
The common room of a small home, a fire in the hearth and children sleeping upstairs.
The backyard of a local manor, in the shade of a large willow tree.
A long table in the civic archives of the city library.
The local theatre before rehearsal. A partial set is on the stage, and crew casually watch from the balcony.
The cellar of the local temple, between aging casks of wine
A small cave obscured by hanging moss, just outside town.
On the deck of a large fishing ship, tied up at the docks.
A dank overflow chamber of the city sewer.
A family mausoleum towards the back of the city cemetery.

name: Guildhalls: Moderate Guildhall
rows: A white walled guildhall with paper windows and thick, heavy shutters.
A rustic guildhall made of notched logs topped by a thatched roof.
A two-storey guildhall of painted green stone set at the end of a muddy lane.
A musty smelling guildhall with thin wooden walls, terrible drafts and too few fireplaces.
A simple brick guildhall with white windows and several tall chimneys.
An old remodelled bakery that still smells of bread and flour.
This guildhall has beige stone walls on the outside and oak wood panelling within.
A guildhall with fieldstone walls and large open rooms.
A squat, brick guildhall with very few windows and a rooftop deck.
The outer walls of this guildhall are set on a stone foundation of an old temple. The new construction is of wood.
A wooden building resting on thick columns. One can only enter when the stairs are lowered.
A stone complex surrounded by an iron fence and small courtyard.
A red walled building with a large central fire pit producing thick black smoke.
A fieldstone building with a thick layer of moss covering its south side.
A wooden two-storey guildhall with ill-fitting windows.
A small stone tower, with a winding central staircase.
A squat stone guildhall of gnomish construction, extending underground through a network of low, cramped passageways and chambers.
An old family home with closed heavy wooden shutters and six locks on the front door.
A well-kept wooden structure with a pointed roof of green shingles.
A small stone guildhall with a large private patio in the rear for hosting social functions.

name: Guildhalls: Motivations
intro: Most guild members join because learning the trade and getting work outside the trade is far more difficult, but what is the guild striving towards in the greater sense? Economic domination is the simple answer, but guild leaders may have something else in mind. (Normal guild members may not know of this additional goal).
rows: To gain respect in court for the guild leaders.
To gain the respect of the community.
To become untouchable by the local militia.
To fund a secret (possibly illegal or reviled) faith or church.
To protect their members where the government has failed.
To educate the masses perhaps through formal schooling, scholarships or similar initiatives.
To advance society and to provide charitable works such as fountains, pools and wells usable by the masses.
For the glory of their lord
To become greater than their foreign rival by producing better products, destroying their rivals trading network and so on.
To reclaim glory after having fallen from favour (perhaps due to some terrible crime or failing of the guild).
To ensure their craft is never forgotten and always held in high regard.
To control the town or city through wealth and bribery.
To know divinity through perfection of their craft.
To win the love of a highborn lady or lord.

name: Guildhalls: Prosperous Guildhall
rows: A large stone guildhall with great woven banners decorating the halls.
A white walled building with stone columns ringing the ground floor that support a promenade balcony above.
A looming stone building with copper embellishments along the windows and doors.
An old manor with two rows of statue flanking the walkway to the main entrance. Gargoyles leer down from the roof.
A squat stone building that leads down to a multilayered complex of dwarven design.
A highly defensible complex with high outer walls, reinforced stone door and an entranceway equipped with murder holes.
A grand tower with pointed slate roof and stained glass windows. Deep cellars below the tower intersect with the town's sewers.
A sprawling manor set among well-tended grounds. Some areas are in disrepair and cluttered with thick spider webs.
A grand building with pink walls, red shutters and tall fountains in the front courtyard surrounded by beautifully tended formal gardens.
A large stone structure with walls reinforced by adamantine. Ornate cold iron gates provide a glimpse of the building beyond.
A three-storey great brick guildhall with a black slate roof and many chimneys.
Large braziers always light the great stone steps outside the entrance of this marbled walled guildhall
A brick guildhall with large stone columns and with trellises covered in ivy.
This guildhall is an odd mix of styles, having once been four distinct buildings. Over the years they were purchased and connected to create a complex of stone and wood of many height and colours.
A gleaming building whose outer walls are a patchwork mosaic of onyx and jade tiles.
A grand stone building with cascading arches connected to support columns.
Large gargoyles of demonic visage guard the roof of this old fieldstone guildhall
This guildhall has large echoing rooms which occasionally make conversations quite difficult.
A great wooden lodge with three stories and a blue shingle roof
A massive oak structure with oil paintings of its members hanging throughout the halls.

name: Guildhalls: Quality
intro: Guildhalls can be anywhere with enough space for the guild to meet, though once a guild achieves a certain level of prosperity they generally obtain a dedicated locale. Use these tables to determine the general characteristics of such a guildhall. You can also add some amenities to make guilds more tempting for players or add flavour to scenes taking place within the guild itself. Every hall at least has a meeting space even if it doubles as one of the amenity rooms.
rows: A {@table Guildhalls: Makeshift Guildhall|RSP|makeshift} guildhall with one {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenity}.
A {@table Guildhalls: Makeshift Guildhall|RSP|makeshift} guildhall with two {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenities}.
A {@table Guildhalls: Moderate Guildhall|RSP|moderate} guildhall with one {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenity}.
A {@table Guildhalls: Moderate Guildhall|RSP|moderate} guildhall with two {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenities}.
A {@table Guildhalls: Moderate Guildhall|RSP|moderate} guildhall with three {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenities}.
A {@table Guildhalls: Prosperous Guildhall|RSP|prosperous} guildhall with three {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenities}.
A {@table Guildhalls: Prosperous Guildhall|RSP|prosperous} guildhall with four {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenities}.
A {@table Guildhalls: Prosperous Guildhall|RSP|prosperous} guildhall with five or more {@table Guildhalls: Amenities|RSP|amenities}.

name: Guildhalls: Rumours
intro: Guilds are very important to the everyday life of an urban society. Even to non-members they often have influence over trade, politics and festivals. People are bound to talk. How much truth can be had in idle gossip is at the GM's discretion.
rows: The guild is secretly controlled by the church.
The guild master's daughter is secretly dating her father's apprentice.
The guild has been working with the thieves' guild to sabotage a rival's business.
The guild waters down its wine at meetings.
The guildhall is built upon the ruins of an ancient vault.
The guild has a secret wing where the true decisions are made.
The guild was responsible for the last king's death.
The guild keeps a private brothel for the exclusive use of its members.
The guild only pretends to be in competition with its rival. It's a carefully controlled show to discourage any real competitors.
The guild master is rarely in town. Instead he investigates old dungeons as an adventurer.
The guild keeps its prices cheap by using undead or slave labour.
The guild has fixed its books to pay less taxes. May local magistrates and tax collectors are paid off or blackmailed into silence.
The guild purchases ill-gotten goods from pirates and uses the profits to fund its members' lavish lifestyles.
The guild practices minor sacrifices to gain the favour of its long dead founders.
The guild's founder is still running things as a reclusive vampire.
The mayor is secretly in the guild's pocket and is on its payroll.
The guild has been training its members to fight, in order to end a rivalry through force of arms.
The guild does new product testing at the local orphanage.
The guild is heavily in debt to foreign investors and desperate for a solution.
The guild moves its goods at night through a series of secret tunnels.

name: Guildhalls: Types of Guilds
intro: A guild is an association of people who practice a craft or labour, who come together to control that practise in a town or larger region. Though they often control the trade through sheer numbers and economic coordination, it was not uncommon for the guild to be granted official authority by the local ruler, making it illegal to practice without membership.
rows: Craft Guild: This is a typical medieval guild. The craft guild comprises skilled artisans who all create items of the same type. Depending on the size of the city and economy it could be as broad as a 'metalworkers' guild, or as specific as a silversmith or coopers' guild.

Merchant Guild: Merchant guilds may be organized by type of product, region or trade routes. They're primarily an organization for those who sell physical products, though some regulate skilled labourers such as physicians or tinkers.

Cartel: A cartel is an organization of craftsmen and/or merchants with the specific intent to fix prices, production and/or public image. Many other guilds are also cartels or a cartel may include members of various other guilds.

Trade/Labour Union: A far less  common type of guild. These unions comprised the lower skilled, or at least the less stationed, members of a craft or labour to protect their common interests and help combat the power of other guilds. These may be more common in societies with large Adventurers Guilds to help organize the many hirelings employed in such endeavours.

Religious Guild: Priests, clerics and the like have their own orders and churches. They have much of the same traits of a guild but their focus usually puts economics second to piety. Religious guilds are still common amongst laypeople, such as when all craftspeople among multiple fields come together under the banner of a common god. Like cartels, often another type of guild will also be a religious guild.

Frith Guild: A group of upstanding citizens who pass judgement on the law. These individuals are often nobles or appointed by the ruling lord. Some frith guilds are actually secret societies, with their own laws that carry out vigilante justice against those who wrong their members and escape normal justice.

Scholars'/Masters' Guild: A predecessor to universities, these are associations of masters, or their students, throughout a city. They are often from completely different fields but united by status and their love of academic study. They are centres of learning.

Adventurers' Guild: Job postings, cheap beds, good beer and the rights to legally loot abandoned structures; an adventurer's guild is a PC's second home in the city. Particularly popular in areas surrounded by ruins or towns with a weak military presence.

Arcanist Guild: Much like a masters' guild, the arcanists' guild is the foundation schools spring from. Arcanists guilds are often supported by governments as a matter of public safety, providing oversight as young mages learn the proper ways of spells and incantations.

Bardic Guild: Loremasters, jesters, storytellers, dancers, actors, playwrights and even the classic adventuring bard all belong to the bardic guild. It's the best place to find work, obtain public performance permits and swap stories.

Companion Guild: Formal organization of prostitutes, courtiers and courtesans. As a profession that needs very little to get started, practitioners organize into guilds more often in large societies with minimal laws, as a means of protection, or in heavily affluent societies were formal training is needed as a matter of course.
Thieves' Guild: A breeding ground for those who act outside of society and ignore property laws. It's the best place to find a fence, pick up speciality tools or grab a job.
Assassins' Guild: Much like the thieves' guild the assassins' guild generally operates outside the law, though some may be government sponsored.

Fraternity/Sorority: An organization dedicated to the development and prosperity of its members. These organizations often cross-occupational boundaries but are bound by a deep devotion to each member. While not technically economic in nature, wealth and prosperity go hand in hand.

Racial Guild: Much like a fraternity or sorority but bound by a common blood. These organizations focus on a single minority race in a society, but may also be applied to another type of guild, such as the Guild of Halfling Weavers.

Secret Society: Not all organizations flourish in the public eye. When popular culture or the law frowns upon how you wish to get things done secret societies form to provide like-minded individuals a place to do business. Cartels, thieves' guilds and assassins' guilds are often secret but any kind of guild can be secret. Some secret societies even have a public face, but keep their rites and dealings known only to members.

name: Gutter Gnoll Lair Details
intro: An area controlled by gutter gnolls might display the following:
rows: A buried cache of foul-smelling meat and a gnawed leather boot
An almost overwhelming musky stench emanates from a corner, a mixture of rotten meat, stagnant mud and raw sewage
Water constantly drips from the ceiling into a filthy, slowly spreading, brown pool
The floor is covered in a thick layer of soft furnishings at various levels of decay and destruction
Fist-sized clumps of matted hair dot the area
A collection of broken and discarded items hang crooked on the walls in a crude mockery of a picture gallery
Reeking piled linens form a nest so soiled that the imprint of a curled gnoll remains clearly defined
A stagnant pool, lumps of foulness collect in the stillness.
A barrel of beer bearing the stamp of a nearby tavern stands next to a few beer-soaked scraps of wood from another, some of which have been chewed
A territory marker cobbled together from a guard's polearm, sackcloth, browning bones, and a jagged-toothed skull

name: Gutter Gnoll Trinkets
intro: The following items might be carried by a gutter gnoll:
rows: A child's doll, torn and filthy
A burlap sack containing dozens of assorted buttons
A leather bucket containing a few belt buckles
A silk scarf, cleaner than its surroundings
A collection of miscellaneous receipts, promissory notes and invoices
An elegant, fashionable hat with the top knocked out
A string of assorted cutlery worn as a necklace
A hessian sack of spoiled meat and old leather
An ale horn, tied to a belt with a shoelace

name: Gynosphinx
rows: The long leonine tail of a sphinx is incredibly distinctive and carries a great amount of cultural significance in some circles. Some sects and cults have a ritual of encasing the tail in dark wax and burning it as a candle wick. It is said that the visions they see in these seances reveal long forgotten secrets buried by time. Others say that sphinx fur just has a mild hallucigenic effect. Unfortunately, there is a distinct dearth of samples to test these hypotheses.
The heart of a sphinx is quite literally full with secrets and mystery. Skilled artificers can bring out this magic in the form of an amulet to aid those who have managed to defeat the sphinx.
The sphinx pelt is both regal and mysterious. Those who wear it share in the noble countenance of the creature they have felled, as well as their independence from time and space.
The eyes of the gynosphinx are bewitching, and even in death they seem to gaze back and burrow deep into your thoughts and secrets.

The majestic wings of a sphinx rival that of celestial angels themselves. Like many magical wings, they make prime base materials for a set of artificial wings that grant the power of flight. These ones however have the added bonus of their sphinx owner's abilities of teleportation.

name: Hadrosaurus
rows: The oddly ridged skull of a hadrosaurus is quite sturdy and is the perfect shape to act as a helmet for horses and other mounts.

name: Hag Patron Expanded Spell List
rows: {@spell create or destroy water}, {@spell fog cloud}
{@spell animal friendship}, {@spell tasha's hideous laughter||hideous laughter}
{@spell lightning bolt}, {@spell leomund's tiny hut||tiny hut}
{@spell Mordenkainen's Faithful Hound||faithful hound}, {@spell phantasmal killer}
{@spell evard's black tentacles||black tentacles}, {@spell control water}

name: Halaster's Gates
rows: The gate is touched with a magic wand with at least 1 charge remaining.
A gold coin is fed into the coin slot.
The gate is touched with a dead twig or branch.
The gate is touched with a nonmagical item made of ferrous metal, such as iron. The item is then reduced to powder and the gate opens.
The gate is tapped thrice by a staff of any kind.
A gemstone worth at least 100 gp is placed in the dragon's mouth, which animates and consumes the gemstone, destroying it.
The horn of the {@creature unicorn|MM} is inserted into the moon symbol.
An interpretive dance replicating the dwarves, which takes 1 minute to perform.
A creature flies or levitates within 5 feet.
An {@condition invisible} creature stands before the mirror.
A pint of any liquid is poured on the floor within 5 feet of the gate.
The key originally held by Rizzeryl on Level 2 must be inserted into the keyhole.
Casting the {@spell mage hand} cantrip and pressing its spectral fingers into the indentation for 1 minute.
A creature sings a D note or plays a D note on a {@item musical instrument|PHB}.
A {@spell silence} spell includes the arch in its area.
The riddle's answer ("O") is said aloud.
A lit torch is brought within 5 feet of the gate.
A character speaks the words, "Way out!" while pointing at the gate.
The correct gear is popped into place, which is noticed with a {@dc 15} Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) check.
A character wears King Melair's crystal crown within 5 feet of the gate (found in Level 6, 11D).
An open book is held within 5 feet of the gate, which then disintegrates.
Speaking the command word ("Axallian") which can be learned by casting {@spell speak with dead|PHB} on any of the skulls woven into the frame.
A creature marked with a bloody X stands within 5 feet of the gate.
A creature targeted by the {@spell maze} spell must become trapped then escape the maze.
Three humanoids hold hands while standing within 5 feet of the gate.
The magical jigsaw piece (revealed via {@spell detect magic|PHB} or drawn on a {@dice d100} result of 1).
A six-fingered gauntlet, which can be found in Area 14B, Level 15, is touched to the gate.
A real, illusory, or artistic depiction of a dragon touches the gate.
An arrow or crossbow bolt shot between the standing stones
The command word ("Kelserath") is uttered, divulged by a sleeping demon or {@spell legend lore} spell.
A magic item of uncommon rarity or rarer is sacrificed

name: Halaster's Top 10
rows: Apocalyptica's {@i Hall of the Mountain King}
Blues Saraceno's {@i Run On For a Long Time}

items: Best described as sinister yet whimsical
Imagined as the adventurers constantly fleeing Halaster's wrath or monsters
Really epitomizes their relationship with Halaster, doesn't it?
Jazz with a hint of cynicism
Provides a well-needed warning: never, never die
High tense jazz, perfect montage music
A melodic power metal song, if your players are into that
Paints Undermountain as a place of perpetual sorrow, its residents unable to escape the Mad Mage's antics

name: Halastron's Favored Phrases
rows: "Rejoice—you are all cogs in the great machine."
"Extinction is inevitable. Live it up while you can."
"I can dig it." / "Can you dig it?"

name: Half Dragon

entries: While regular dragon blood is too foreign to have any effect on a humanoid without significant alteration, the diluted nature of a half-dragon's blood allows it to bestow significant benefits on a humanoid imbiber.

entries.name: Use:
entries: As an action you may drink the vial of half-dragon blood. For the next 10 minutes, you gain the same type of damage resistance of the half-dragon it was taken from.

rows: Half-dragons occupy an odd position in the taxonomy of creatures. This is best reflected in the strange effect that their bodies have on the senses of real dragons around them. Their strange physiology seems to cause them to slip beneath the notice of dragons of their own colour, tricking them into thinking they are one of their own. Taking a half-dragon's scales, grinding them into a powder, and then mixing them with oil creates a paste that other humanoids can apply to their own bodies to avoid or promote detection by dragons.

name: Half-Ogre
rows: The blood of a regular ogre is too foreign and extreme to be compatible with that of a humanoid's system. A half-ogre on the other hand has the perfect dilution of humanoid blood for it to not be toxic to a humanoid, while still conferring the power of its giant progenitor.

name: Harmful Mutations
intro: Unless noted otherwise, the following mutations are visible, obvious, and grotesque. They offer no benefits, only drawbacks. None of them require you to use an action.
rows: {@b Deformed leg:} Your speed on foot is reduced by 5 feet. You must succeed on a DC 10 Dexterity saving throw after using the Dash action. If you fail the save, you fall prone.

{@b Deformed face/appearance:} You are deformed or disfigured to the extent that it can't be easily concealed. You have disadvantage on Charisma (Persuasion) checks and advantage on Charisma (Intimidation) checks.
{@b Deformed arm/hand:} You have disadvantage with any roll requiring you to use that arm or hand (including wielding two-handed weapons).
{@b Malformed brain:} You have disadvantage on all Intelligence checks.
{@b Mentally vulnerable:} You have disadvantage on Intelligence saving throws.
{@b Slow and lumbering:} You have disadvantage on all Dexterity checks.
{@b Sickly:} You have disadvantage on all Constitution saving throws.

{@b Horrible growth:} A large goiter, immobile tendril, or useless extra eye hangs from your face. You have disadvantage on Charisma (Persuasion) checks and advantage on Charisma (Intimidation) checks.

{@b Useless limb:} One of your limbs is unusable or missing. If it's your arm, you can no longer hold anything with two hands, and you can hold only a single object at a time. If it's your leg, your speed on foot is halved, you must use a cane or crutch to move unless you have a peg leg or other prosthesis, you fall prone after using the Dash action, and you have disadvantage on Dexterity checks made to balance.
{@b Useless eye:} One of your eyes is unusable or missing. You have disadvantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on sight and on ranged attack rolls.
{@b Useless ear:} One of your ears is unusable or missing. You have disadvantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on hearing.
{@b Weakness in Strength:} You have disadvantage on all Strength checks and attack rolls that use your Strength modifier.
{@b Weakness in Dexterity:} You have disadvantage on all Dexterity checks and attack rolls that use your Dexterity modifier.
{@b Weakness in mind:} This affects your Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma (equal chances). You have disadvantage on all checks and attack rolls using that ability score.

name: Harpy
rows: Harpy feathers are notably large but of a fine quality, reflective of the harpies beautiful but dangerous nature. Too large for fletching, they nonetheless make excellent quills.

If harpies are known for one thing, it is their singing. Their vocal cords are able to produce a wide variety of sounds, and some daring bards have taken to using them as strings for their instruments. Bards with instruments of the harpies are said to play music that can entrance entire rooms of listeners.

On a rare occasion, you may slay a harpy that was in the middle of ovulation. Whether the egg is fertilised is irrelevant, as it is the eggshell that holds the true value. When this pink-speckled shell is powdered, it makes a dye with potent magical abilities.

entries.name: Call of the Grave
entries: An angel of death is obsessed with your fleeting spirit, and wants you back. When you roll initiative at the start of combat, make a death {@quickref saving throws|PHB|2|1|saving throw}. On a failed save, the GM chooses an undead creature with a CR equal to your level or lower. It appears at a point 120 feet away from you and joins the combat against you. The creature knows where you are at all times and pursues you unerringly. It vanishes when reduced to 0 hit points, when you die, or after 10 minutes.

entries.name: Memories from the Beyond
entries: The memory of death lingers. At the end of each {@quickref resting|PHB|2|0|long rest}, describe how your character has tried to forget what dying felt like, then make a Wisdom {@quickref saving throws|PHB|2|1|saving throw} with a DC set by the GM based on your answer. On a failed save, you gain one level of {@condition exhaustion} that lasts until you are subject to {@spell greater restoration} or similar magic, or until you spend 30 days in focused downtime to make peace with your memories.

entries.name: Obscure Purpose
entries: A greater power allowed you to come back for a reason. This might be a god such as the {@deity The Matron of Ravens|Exandria|TalDoreiCampaignSettingReborn|Matron of Ravens} that you can now commune with, or an obscure supernatural being. This consequence might be an opportunity to become a {@class cleric} or {@class paladin} of this god, or to take levels in the {@class warlock} class. Alternatively, if you choose not to swear a covenant with this entity, or if you disobey their requests, roll again on this table. You suffer the new consequences until you adhere to the purpose of this entity or find a way to rid yourself of their attention.

entries.name: Persistent Wounds
entries: Whenever you fail a death {@quickref saving throws|PHB|2|1|saving throw}, your hit point maximum is reduced by {@dice 2d10} until you finish a {@quickref resting|PHB|2|0|long rest}. If your hit point maximum is reduced to 0 in this way, you die.

entries.name: Secret Face
entries: You are no longer you, but a chaotic evil shapechanger who has taken your place. You play this duplicate and use your original game statistics until the duplicate is killed or until this consequence is otherwise overcome. The GM determines where your soul is actually being held captive—possibly in the afterlife for which you were intended, or in your double's malign realm.

entries.name: Hunger for Death
entries: Once per day, you or the GM must decide that you use the following reaction: When you see a creature you perceive as hostile or potentially hostile and your distance to that creature is equal to or less than your speed, you immediately and aggressively move your speed toward that creature, then make one melee attack against it. You have {@quickref Advantage and Disadvantage|PHB|2|0|advantage} on the attack roll if your attack is unexpected.

entries.name: Opaque Thoughts
entries: You obsessively recall the sensation of life tearing you from the jaws of death. These ever-present memories fill your mind, making you immune to any effect that would sense your emotions or read your thoughts. Likewise, other creatures have {@quickref Advantage and Disadvantage|PHB|2|0|disadvantage} on Wisdom ({@skill Insight}) checks made to ascertain your intentions.

entries.name: Unearthly Awareness
entries: Your ordeal left a mark upon your soul, which now shudders in the presence of the undead. You know whenever an undead creature is within 30 feet of you, and you don't have {@quickref Advantage and Disadvantage|PHB|2|0|disadvantage} on attacks against {@condition invisible} undead within this range. This constant awareness is distracting, however, and you have {@quickref Advantage and Disadvantage|PHB|2|0|disadvantage} on Intelligence ({@skill Investigation}) and Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) checks while any undead creature is within 30 feet of you.

entries.name: Bond of Vengeance
entries: You have returned as a revenant, bearing an unquenchable spark of hatred for the creature that killed you. As an action, you can focus on this spark to immediately learn the distance and direction to any creature that has killed you. If that creature is on a different plane, you learn only that information. If a creature that killed you dies, you immediately know. If you are within 120 feet of a creature that killed you, you have {@quickref Advantage and Disadvantage|PHB|2|0|disadvantage} on attack rolls against any other creature.

entries.name: Never Again
entries: You don't fall unconscious when reduced to 0 hit points. Instead, you remain conscious until you end your turn without having attacked a creature or cast a spell of 1st level or higher. While you have 0 hit points, you have {@quickref Advantage and Disadvantage|PHB|2|0|advantage} on attack rolls, your attacks deal an extra {@damage 1d10} damage on a hit, and attack rolls made against you have {@quickref Advantage and Disadvantage|PHB|2|0|disadvantage}. You make death {@quickref saving throws|PHB|2|1} as normal, including suffering a failure when you take damage. Additionally, whenever you take damage while at 0 hit points, your hit point maximum is reduced by an amount equal to the damage until you finish a {@quickref resting|PHB|2|0|long rest}.

name: Harvester Domain Spells
footnotes: {@note Spells marked with an * are from {@loader Hamund's Harvesting Handbook Volume 2|collection/Jasmine Yang; Hamund's Harvesting Handbook II.json}.}

entries: When a hell hound dies, it is consumed by its internal fire leaving nothing behind but ash of burnt fur. While this is disappointing to harvesters, the fur still has some utility.

entries.name: Use:
entries: As an action, you may rub 1 tuft of hell hound fur into your hands. If you do so, for the next minute, whenever you roll a 1 or 2 on a fire damage dice roll, you may reroll that die and you must use the new number. After being used, the tuft of hell hound fur loses its magic and becomes useless.

name: Hellfire Engine

entries: Deep in the pits of Avernus lay the Bonemelt Pools: vast formations of roiling red oil that burn with all the intensity that the Nine Hells can muster. Every day, legions of lower devils are sent into these pools to pump this corrosive liquid into barrels that are then loaded into the dreaded hellfire engines to be sprayed indiscriminately on the enemies of its master. {@b Requires {@item enchanted vial|HHHVI}.}

entries.name: Use:
entries: As an action you may make a ranged weapon attack to throw a vial of bonemelt oil at a target within 20 feet, shattering it on impact, treating the vial as an improvised {@homebrew weapon|object}. On a hit, the target is drenched in oil and take {@damage 1d10} fire damage plus {@damage 2d8} acid damage at the end of their turns. If an affected creature suffers fire damage that was not caused by this oil, the oil combusts, causing the covered creature to instantly suffer {@damage 2d10} fire damage and {@damage 4d8} acid damage and removing the oil. An affected creature or another creature within 5 feet can also take an action to scrape off the oil.

rows: The lightning flail of the hellfire engine is a mighty weapon to behold, dreamed up in the nefarious workshops of the Nine Hells. The key component responsible for its shockingly destructive power is a piece of hellforged metal known as the hellbolt coil. This coil is capable of channeling the inherent energy of the multiverse to create electrical surges that the hellfire engine then channels into its flail. Particularly talented tinkers are capable of reverse engineering this infernal technology into incredibly deadly weapons made for mortal hands.

When a hellfire engine wishes to destroy a target from far away it relies on the thunder cannon. This incredibly destructive armament carries a stronger payload that damages targets far beyond the initial impact zone of the blast, especially when compared to regular cannon shot. Despite common belief, this power comes not from the shot itself, but the enchanted cannon barrel that launches it. This "shock barrel", as it has been dubbed by fiendish scholars, is engraved with devilish runes that enchant any ammunition stored within. Thankfully, an intact barrel can easily be repurposed for use by a mortal adventurer, allowing them to use projectiles that strike with the impact of a thunderclap.

entries: At the center of a hellfire engine lies the infamous hellfire core: a coconut-sized, superheated ball of black steel forged in fires fueled by the immolation of hundreds of mortal souls. This core acts as the engine's "essence", functioning much like the brain and heart of a normal creature. Due to its horrid crafting method, this core constantly hungers for more souls and is responsible for the reaping, consumption, and transformation of the souls that the engine destroys.

entries.name: Use:
entries: When you kill a creature while holding this item, you may use your reaction to hold the core over their corpse. If you do so, the core absorbs the recently deceased soul of the creature and destroys it over the course of {@dice 1d4} days. If the creature isn't revived before then, only a {@spell wish} spell can restore it to life. Constructs and devils are immune to this effect.

name: Helmed Horror
rows: When crafting a helmed horror, no ordinary helmet will do. One made specifically for the purpose must be commissioned in order to grant the unique senses that the helmed horror possesses. With some time, an artificer can take one of these helms and reconfigure the arcane signatures so that they work for regular humanoids.

entries: The animating spirit of a helmed horror dissipates quickly after its form loses structural integrity. If done quickly however, this spirit can be caught using a sheet of {@item spirit paper|HHHVI}. No matter how quick you may be however, some of the spirit will have degraded already, thus any attempt at reusing the spirit is sure to result in a lower quality construct than the original helmed horror. {@b Requires {@item spirit paper|HHHVI}.}

entries.name: Use:
entries: You may spend an hour performing a {@dc 15} Intelligence ({@skill Arcana}) check with the {@item spirit paper|HHHVI} to transfer the essence to an unworn suit of {@item plate armor|PHB}. If you are successful, the essence leaves the {@item spirit paper|HHHVI} and enters the suit of armor, creating an {@creature animated armor} under your control. This armor follows your instructions to the best of its ability, but lacks the intelligence to discern any nuance from your words and follows orders to the letter. This {@creature animated armor} remains until it is destroyed.

name: Helviti Comanda
rows: Gold Comanda are noble and diligent. They prefer close quarters combat with swords and shields.
Wendigo Helviti are independent and often operate alone or in groups of two to three. They prefer ranged combat and ambush tactics.
Fearsome siege experts. They operate in kill-squads and often carry small portable ballista with them in battle in groups of three.

Ravaged at the {@book Battle of Looming Rock|BITCEH|1|The Battle at Looming Rock}, this noble Comanda is greatly reduced in strength. They prioritise fierce independence and draw their tactics from the Northern Kingdom barbarians.
Naval experts, possibly the only Comanda to specialise in such a role.
Specialists in setting up fortifications and outposts. Often hired alongside settlers to efficiently build settlements in hostile areas.

name: Herb's Relative Rarity Table
footnotes: {@note First column added to enable 5eTools style rollable table.}

name: Herbal Brews
caption: Compounds: Herbal Brews
footnotes: {@note * see the {@variantrule Formulas|CompEquipMan} variant rule}

name: Herbalism Harvesting Mishaps
caption: HerbalismHarvest
rows: You cut your hand on thorns, take 1d6 piercing damage
You develop a burning rash from the plant, take {@damage 1d6} fire damage.
You accidentally smear acidic sap on your hand, take {damage 1d6} acid damage.
You inhale a cloud of spores from the plant, take 1d6 psychic damage
You ingest the wrong part of the plant, take 1d6 poison damage
All warmth in your hand is drawn into the plant, take 1d6 cold damage
Necrotizing bacteria from the plant touches your hand, take 1d6 necrotic damage
You have a bad reaction that makes you feel weak, disadvantage on strength checks for 1 hour
You have a bad reaction that makes you feel dizzy, disadvantage on dexterity checks for 1 hour
You have a bad reaction that makes you feel nauseous, disadvantage on constitution checks for 1 hour
You have a bad reaction that makes you feel confused, disadvantage on intelligence checks for 1 hour
You have a bad reaction that makes you feel forgetful, disadvantage on wisdom checks for 1 hour
You have a bad reaction that makes you feel lethargic, disadvantage on charisma checks for 1 hour
You have a bad reaction that makes you feel shaky, disadvantage on attack rolls for 1 hour
you have a bad reaction that makes you feel stiff, your move speed is halved for 1 hour
You have a bad reaction that makes your tongue and lips swell, you cannot speak comprehensibly for 1 hour
An unusual reaction makes your muscles buzz with energy, advantage on strength checks for 1 hour
An unusual reaction makes you feel energized, advantage on dexterity checks for 1 hour
An unusual reaction invigorates your body, advantage on constitution checks for 1 hour
An unusual reaction clears your mind, advantage on intelligence checks for 1 hour
An unusual reaction reveals hidden information, advantage on wisdom checks for 1 hour
An unusual reaction loosens your tongue and lightens your mood, advantage on charisma checks for 1 hour
An unusual reaction improves your reaction time, advantage on attack rolls for 1 hour
An unusual reaction imbues you with speed, your move speed is doubled for 1 hour
An unusual reaction causes you to secrete a slippery substance, advantage on checks made to escape being grappled for 1 hour

name: Herbalism Prices
caption: Herbalism Prices
colLabels: {@dice 1d100 + #$prompt_number:min=0,title=Enter the Modifier from Selling Herbalism Ingredients table,$#|d100 + Mod}
rows: A buyer offering a tenth of the base price
A buyer offering a fifth of the base price, and a shady buyer offering half of the base price
A buyer offering to purchase all of your ingredients at once at half price
A shady buyer who is willing to buy all of your ingredients at full price, no questions asked

name: Hezrou
rows: The spiny, shark-like teeth of the hezrou. Menacing when attached to an implement of torture, but their irregular formation makes them useful for little else.

The blood of the hezrou is as thick and sludgy as week old garbage, and smells just as bad. If you have the stomach for it however, ingesting it with a few neutralising herbs temporarily inoculates the body to foul miasmas and effluents.

entries: The rank stench of the hezrou lingers in one's memory long after they have already been removed from its presence. Removing this gland without rupturing it takes an extraordinarily steady hand, but once harvested, can be thrown as a quick and dirty bomb.

entries.name: Use:
entries: As an action you may throw this item at a point within 20 feet, causing it to explode on impact. Any creature within 10 feet of that point must succeed on a {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw or be {@condition poisoned} until the start of its next turn.

rows: The enormous claw of the hezrou. Incredibly sharp, and never seems to dull. Can be forged into a powerful and intimidating weapon.
{@filter Any +2 melee piercing weapon|items|source=|type=melee weapon|category=|weapon damage type=p|bonus=weapon attack and damage rolls (+2)}

entries: The Oasis is an animal sanctuary, hidden in a small valley surrounded by hills. It is filled with antelopes, boars, goats, camels, foxes, lizards, sparrows, falcons, and a few frogs. The Oasis is protected from predators by a {@creature Pack of Lions|SandsOfDoom} ({@adventure Appendix B|SandsOfDoom|13}), who sit atop an elevated stone butte, gazing at their territory. Every once in a while, the lions kill one of the beasts to feed.

entries.name: Finding the Oasis
entries: The characters encounter several animals, all peaceful and traveling in the same direction. Following the animals leads to the sanctuary.

The Oasis is a small shrine dedicated to the Aru, hidden within a canyon. Blessed by the Aru thousands of years ago, the shrine has kept the Rust from seeping into the nearby soil. Choose one between these two Interesting Finds: {@adventure Obelisk of Anubia|SandsOfDoom|6|Obelisk of Anubia} or {@adventure Speaking Statue of the Sphinx|SandsOfDoom|6|Speaking Statue of the Sphinx}. The shrine features the chosen Interesting Find in addition to having the benefits of an Oasis.

entries.name: Finding the Oasis
entries: {@adventure Divine Relics|SandsOfDoom|14} in the characters' possession start to glow with radiant power, growing brighter as they approach the shrine. The characters gain {@variantrule Heroic Inspiration|XPHB} once they find it.

The Oasis is located within a sandy cave, inhabited by Sand Spirits who gather to drink water and share gossip about events in the Wasteland. These spirits have built a miniature town entirely out of sand around the spring. They are friendly and can answer up to five questions from the characters. However, if the characters damage the sand village, the spirits grow resentful and hostile, behaving as though drunk (see {@adventure Sand Spirits|SandsOfDoom|2|Sand Spirits})

entries.name: Finding the Oasis
entries: The characters hear the whispers of the Sand Spirits carried by the wind blowing from the direction of the cave.

The Oasis blooms within the skeleton of an  {@creature Ancient Brass Dragon|XMM} found at the base of a tall cliffside. The water spring flourishes inside the dragon's rib cage, while palm trees grow through its eye sockets. Even after the dragon's death, the Oasis continues to be affected by the magical regional effects linked to a brass dragon's presence (see its entry in the Monster Manual). Illusory images of dinosaurs can be seen wandering around the Oasis, gathering near the dragon's skeletal remains as if in mourning.

entries.name: Finding the Oasis
entries: Magical tracks formed in the sand guide the characters to the Oasis (part of the brass dragon's regional effect).

The shrine features the chosen Interesting Find in addition to having the benefits of an Oasis.

entries.name: Finding the Oasis
entries: {@adventure Divine Relics|SandsOfDoom14|14} in the characters' possession start to glow with radiant power, growing brighter as they approach the shrine. The characters gain {@variantrule Inspiration|DMG} once they find it.

The Oasis is located within a sandy cave, inhabited by Sand Spirits who gather to drink water and share gossip about events in the Wasteland. These spirits have built a miniature town entirely out of sand around the spring. They are friendly and can answer up to five questions from the characters. However, if the characters damage the sand village, the spirits grow resentful and hostile, behaving as though drunk (see {@adventure Sand Spirits|SandsOfDoom14|2|Sand Spirits})

entries.name: Finding the Oasis
entries: The characters hear the whispers of the Sand Spirits carried by the wind blowing from the direction of the cave.

The Oasis blooms within the skeleton of an  {@creature Ancient Brass Dragon|MM} found at the base of a tall cliffside. The water spring flourishes inside the dragon's rib cage, while palm trees grow through its eye sockets. Even after the dragon's death, the Oasis continues to be affected by the magical regional effects linked to a brass dragon's presence (see its entry in the Monster Manual). Illusory images of dinosaurs can be seen wandering around the Oasis, gathering near the dragon's skeletal remains as if in mourning.

entries.name: Finding the Oasis
entries: Magical tracks formed in the sand guide the characters to the Oasis (part of the brass dragon's regional effect).

name: Hill Giant
rows: Resembling the brush on the top of a barren hill, the hair of a hill giant is considered a valuable resource to leatherworkers. The hair of a hill giant, while unpleasant to the touch, makes for a good rope material and even the hill giants themselves use it to stitch their clothes together.

Like all giants, the fingernail of the hill giant is a key component in brewing the ubiquitous potion of giant strength. Despite the misconception among adventurers who believe that felling one giant can supply them potions for life, only one potion can be brewed per giant. This is because the alchemical process uses the fingernail as a channeling foci to summon that particular giant's strength and thus renders any other attempts moot.

name: Hippogriff
rows: The hooves of a hippogriff contain a unique collagen in them that when rendered creates a high quality adhesive. This glue is prized by leatherworkers and most can never find enough to meet their demand.
The pristine feathers of a hippogriff carry an almost supernatural aerodynamic quality to them. Fletchers and sharpshooters prize good condition hippogriff feathers for fletching high quality arrows.

It is said that a hippogriff can spot a mouse in a field from more than 2 miles over. Whether true or not, they can definitely spot an orcish ambush coming from a few hundred feet out, and this is another reason that hippogriffs are so highly valued as mounts and companions.

name: Hobgoblin
rows: The body of a hobgoblin holds little practical use for harvesters. Most cities however will pay small bounties for hobgoblin ears.

name: Hobgoblin Captain
rows: The body of a hobgoblin holds little practical use for harvesters. Most cities however will pay small bounties for hobgoblin ears.

As a hobgoblin grows in experience and prestige, they grow out their hair into braids that are only ever cut if they lose a battle. These braids hold some value to collectors as well as bounty offices as proof of felling a noteworthy hobgoblin threat.

As a hobgoblin grows in experience and prestige, they grow out their hair into braids that are only ever cut if they lose a battle. These braids hold some value to collectors as well as bounty offices as proof of felling a noteworthy hobgoblin threat.

When a hobgoblin becomes powerful enough that they are considered a warlord, they receive a special mark to venerate themselves in the face of their deity: {@deity Maglubiyet|Nonhuman|PHB}. If skinned correctly and preserved, this mark can be taken by thaumaturges to craft a trinket imbued with the terrifying influence of the goblinoid god.

name: Homunculus
rows: The destroyed body of a homunculus returns to its mundane components upon its death. These components can be recycled into a new homunculus.

entries: The homunculus' blood is the same as its master's: a wizard must bleed onto an empty construct in order to bring it to life. While this imparts a connection to that wizard that they would find useful, it can also be exploited by others skilled in the arcane arts who manage to capture said homunculus. As such, the price of this blood can vary wildly depending on which wizard's homunculus it was taken from. {@b Requires {@item enchanted vial|HHHVI}.}

entries.name: Use:
entries: As an action you may drink the homunculus blood. Doing so gives you all the knowledge that the homunculus had up to the point of its death, including the languages it knew, and the knowledge that its creator shared with it. You may not necessarily understand all of this knowledge, especially if it is of a very esoteric nature and you may not necessarily be able to parse all of it. You retain this knowledge for 10 minutes, after which all of it vanishes from your mind. Once this happens, you become {@condition stunned} for 1 minute as your mind recovers from the influx of information it received.

name: Homunculus Servants
rows: Spits spell along with a song

name: Hooked Horror
rows: The hooked horror's exoskeleton is harder than iron, but unfortunately is difficult to reshape and thus unsuited for armor. However, it does have several other uses including being used as a sturdy container, building material, or even as using its reverberative nature as a percussion instrument. Many Underdark cultures thus value these exoskeletons when recovered in good condition.

The extremely sensitive cochlea of a hooked horror is not unlike that of a bat's. Capable of hearing both extreme distances and different wavelengths, this cochlea serves as a key component for various hearing aids and magical items.

The eponymous hooks of the hooked horror. Formed of an extremely hard, yet yielding, keratin material. With slight modifications, these hooks can be turned into a formidable war pick that doubles as a climbing pick.

name: Hopeful Omens
rows: A bear with pure white fur stands upon a rise, staring up at the stars before wandering away.
The sun, warm and bright, pierces through the overcast skies to illuminate the area around you.
Two ravens wait until you notice them on a nearby perch before croaking and flying away.
A grey wolf appears for a moment, seems to nod to you, then withdraws into shadow.
The sparks rising from the fire twist into familiar runes before scattering into the night.
Nine hand-sized stones form a perfect circle ahead of you.
A single flower blooms amidst the snow, a splash of color against the white.
For a moment, you hear the clicking of the weaver's loom in the wind.
A stranger in a tattered cloak stands in the shadows watching you with a single gleaming eye
You find a small stone with a pattern not unlike a rune scratched upon it by an unknown hand.
A bright, fiery light burns itself across the sky, heading North.
Behold! The Bifrost shimmers in the night sky!

name: Horned Devil
rows: The eponymous horns of the horned devil resemble those of an oversized goat. Extremely hard, they make striking trophies when mounted on one's mantle or displayed in a sacrilegious ritual; whichever is more appealing to you.

Horned devils are noticeably lazy and sluggish, especially for a creature as motivated as a devil. When their blood is mixed with other soporifics, it creates a tonic that can weaken the motivation of even the most stalwart creature.

The tail of the horned devil ends in a vicious barb designed to open wounds and cause a victim to die a slow, painful death. If removed from the horned devil however, the tail can be repurposed into a vicious pike, spear, or whip.
As the horned devil serves as the flying soldier for the armies of the Abyss, their wings are particularly strong and make good crafting material.

name: Horned One Features
rows: {@subclassFeature Expanded Spell List|Warlock|PHB|Horned One|Ar2|1|Ar2}, {@subclassFeature Horned Hunter|Warlock|PHB|Horned One|Ar2|1|Ar2}

name: Hot Items
rows: Multiple parties. Roll twice on this table, rerolling 1s.
A powerful bandit lord has caught wind of the item and is looking to take it for selfish gain.
A valiant hero wishes to see the item returned to the place from whence it came.
The item was stolen from a wealthy noble's collection. The noble has hired experienced bounty hunters to retrieve it.
The item has been magically tied to a legendary entity of great malice that requires it to restore its faded power.

name: How did you Acquire your patron
colLabels: How Did you Acquire your Patron
intro: The following table offers twelve example encounters that brought a warlock and a young patron together.
rows: You found your patron for sale at a black market. When you became aware of one another the connection was instant. Did you purchase your patron or did you obtain them in another way?

While seeking shelter from a storm, you and the patron ended up in the same safe spot. You agreed to share the space while you waited out the storm. During the night, you two struck up a conversation and learned of one another's needs. You agreed to become warlock and patron, and the pair of you have worked together ever since.

The patron's parents became aggressive and had to be put down. You chose to adopt the creature instead of leaving it. Your relationship started off rocky. Has it smoothed out since then, or are things still tense at times?

You found the patron's egg (or its infant form) in the lair of a spellcaster. It appeared as though the spellcaster was going to attempt a ritual on the egg before you defeated them. You cared for the egg and the creature imprinted on you.

On a starlit night in the wilds, you heard a lonesome song across the night air. When you found the source of this harrowing melody, you discovered the patron. What was your patron so forlorn about? Why did you decide to help it?

Your patron was being chased by other, larger creatures that wished to eat it. You intervened and saved them. Over the course of this battle you learned your own abilities were not enough. Your patron offered you a deal and you accepted, becoming their warlock.

An adult version of your patron appeared before you, juvenile patron by their side. They forced your patron upon you, insisting that you help raise it and become its servant. You survived because you agreed to their terms unconditionally.

A friend of yours was the original warlock for your patron. Unfortunately, they died. Why did you become the patron's new warlock? Does the patron attempt to hide how desperately they miss your friend? How has this affected your relationship?

While traveling, you awoke one night to find the patron in your rucksack, devouring your rations and other supplies. The famished creature was initially hostile if you attempted to get your food back. How did you make them trust you? Did you offer more food? Perhaps some water? What about this interaction endeared you enough to become a warlock?

Your patron sought out you in particular. Perhaps they arrived on your doorstep or at your campsite one morning and demanded you swear a pact with them. Why were you chosen? Do you even know? Work out the reason with your Dungeon Master and determine if your warlock is aware of it.

You and your patron died at the exact same time. Both of your deaths were unplanned accidents and the deity of death apologized to you both personally. Unfortunately, they could not revive you both without intermingling your souls. Now you and the patron are forever connected. How do the both of you feel about this arrangement?

While sleeping one night, you had a strange dream. In the dream, the patron reached out to you, asking for your help. Did you try to ignore the dream or readily embrace it? Regardless, you sought out the patron through these mysterious portents and eventually found one another.
